title: Why Is Europe Burning?
excerpt: M. R. O’Connor writes about the devastating wildfires that have engulfed Spain and other parts of Europe.
content_html:
On July 15th, a wildfire broke out near the small town of Orés, Spain, in the northern province of Zaragoza. Propelled by strong winds and low humidity, the flames quickly spread over foothills and through canyons. By the next day, as the fire ballooned to more than eleven thousand acres, five towns in its path had to be evacuated. For José Luis Duce Aragüés, a wildland firefighter whose family is from Zaragoza, news of the fire felt personal. As a teen-ager, he’d spent summers exploring the same mountains that were now burning.

Just two days later, Aragüés, who is based in California but travels internationally to help communities manage fire risk, learned about another blaze. This one, in the nearby Guadalajara province of Spain, was close to where members of his family live today. He’d begun his fire career in Guadalajara, working summers in the small town of Cogolludo. “Everything started for me there,” Aragüés told me. “I started my suppression career there—my first hand crew, first engine crew. I know those mountains, those forests, those trails.” The La Mierla fire, as it came to be known, grew to more than eighty thousand acres. Many of his friends and family in the area either evacuated or worked to combat the flames. His uncle, a retired wildland firefighter, used his heavy machinery to build a firebreak around his farm, and then drove it to a nearby village to offer aid. The size and ferocity of the La Mierla fire disturbed Aragüés, yet the situation was about to get worse. “I couldn’t believe that, when that fire was being controlled, this other fire happened,” he said.

On July 22nd, sparks from a piece of heavy machinery ignited a fire near the town of Burgohondo, in Ávila province. Aragüés had worked in that area, too, for Spain’s Brigadas de Refuerzo en Incendios Forestales—the national firefighting force—and for a fire-prevention team under the country’s Ministry of Environment. This time, the flames spread and merged with a fire that was already burning nearby, in the mountains southwest of Madrid. The conflagrations ultimately crossed into Toledo province and grew into the Burgohondo fire complex—the largest wildfire in Spain’s recorded history, covering more than a hundred and thirty-five thousand acres. One scientist estimated that the complex has released the energy of twenty-three atomic bombs. Aragüés learned that one of his former crewmates, who was defending a friend’s house, lost his own home when the fire travelled down a slope next to him. Another friend, also a firefighter, sent him a text from near the fire: “José, everything we learned, everything we knew, everything that we have been learning for 25 years, means nothing.”

Already this year, more than two hundred thousand hectares have burned in Spain, a figure that is twice than the historical average. France is dealing with a similarly extraordinary fire season. A conflagration west of Bordeaux, described as four times the size of Paris, prompted the largest peacetime evacuation in the country’s history: two hundred and twenty thousand people. Meanwhile, English firefighters have struggled to contain the Tintwistle Moor fire, which is thought to be one of the largest in the country’s recent history. Even as meteorologists warned that a “monstrous, long-lasting” heat wave—Europe’s fourth of the year—was approaching, other fires burned as far north as Sweden and as far south as Crete.

The terrifying news cycle prompted me to open Instagram on a recent evening. Perhaps because I am a qualified wildland firefighter myself, I was quickly blasted with scenes of the fires. I saw horses running for their lives through ghostly, smoke-filled streets; drone footage of charred earth and the husks of homes; and flames engulfing forests as sirens wailed in the distance. Many montages were accompanied by heart-wrenching soundtracks. After an hour of mainlining imagery of infernos, I felt like reality itself had gone up in flames. One scene, of a burning forest under an orange sky, was overlaid with a single word: “L’Apocalypse.” I felt that special sense of doom that descends when humanity is pummelled with disasters.

In “Everything Must Go: The Stories We Tell About the End of the World,” the critic and journalist Dorian Lynskey points out that defeatism is unhelpful, and should not be mistaken for moral seriousness. “The evolutionary purpose of fear is to jolt one into an act of self-preservation,” Lynskey writes, “but one cannot live in a constant state of psychic emergency. The higher the stakes, the less tenable fear is, and the more likely it is to breed dissociation or hopelessness.” He instead calls on readers to resist—“to live in the space between ‘Everything will be OK’ and ‘Everything is fucked,’ between denial and despair.’ ” Lynskey suggests that there might be some way to grasp the significance of events like the unprecedented wildfires in Europe without giving in to dread. For me, the only way to do this is to get curious about why these things are happening. Why are flames erupting in this particular way, in this particular moment in time? Why is Europe burning?

When I put that question to Antonio J. Vera Mena, a Spanish wildland firefighter who has been working in Andalusia as a member of a helicopter-borne brigade, he described a matrix of factors. One of them is extreme heat. Another, paradoxically, was a recent period that was exceptionally wet, which nurtured thick grass in areas that were already overgrown. “We put all these ingredients in a cocktail shaker, and the result is massive fires that far exceed the extinguishing capacity of firefighting teams,” Mena said in an e-mail.

In June, Stephen Pyne, a former wildland firefighter and an emeritus professor of history at Arizona State University, published his forty-sixth book, “Undying Fire: A Fire History of Europe.” When I called him, he posed me one of his central questions about megafires: “Why is it that countries that we think of as modernized—those that have money, science, technology—are the ones that are being clobbered?” Climate change is, of course, part of the story. “Fossil fuels give you power,” Pyne told me, but burning them “disrupts the climate in ways that make fires more powerful.” Extreme fire weather, exceptionally dry, windy, and often warm conditions, is on the rise globally. That said, climate change is happening everywhere—and, in Pyne’s account, only some areas are experiencing worsening fires. This is one of the mysteries he’s interested in.

Pyne argues that Mediterranean Europe, much like California, is naturally predisposed to burn because of an annual cycle of wetting and drying. He writes in “Undying Fire” that, for eons, Europeans used fire to cultivate pastures, farms, woodlands, gardens, and orchards; burning liberated nutrients, cleared space, and promoted desired plants. He calls this practice “pyric horticulture.” And many modern Europeans understand themselves as part of this history. A researcher examining attitudes about wildfire policy once interviewed a resident of the Occitanie region of southern France, which borders Spain. “We often forget that we are in a region, regardless of climate change, which experiences hot and dry summers, with fires which are very, very predominantly of anthropogenic origin,” the resident said. “And it doesn’t come from today, it comes from the time of the Romans and the Greeks.”

By creating mosaic landscapes of interlocking fields, pastures, and orchards, Europeans broke up and thinned out trees and brush, making devastating fires less likely. But, in recent generations, Europe’s rural landscapes have rapidly transformed. Agriculture has industrialized and scaled up; fast-growing tree plantations have spread. Some of the most dramatic footage on social media appears to show the blackened remains of plantation forests: row after row of trees, spaced as evenly as Iowa corn, charred by fire.

The planting of trees is often celebrated, but the details matter. Pyne argues that Europe’s “broken-up biomes” have been “transfigured into monocultures of biomass fuel.” In Spain alone, some four million hectares have been afforested—establishing forest where, historically, there was none—since the nineteen-forties, mostly with flammable species like pine and eucalyptus. Between 1990 and 2015, the portion of Europe that was wooded increased by ninety thousand square kilometres—an area around the size of Portugal. The European Union has committed to planting three billion trees by 2030, in an effort to capture and store carbon. This movement has ecological and social consequences, and flammability is one of them.

The most important way that European landscapes are changing is that unprecedented numbers of people are leaving rural areas, a phenomenon that has accelerated in the last fifty years. “Families leave the forests for the cities,” Mena, the firefighter in southern Spain, said. Jobs are scarce in rural areas, he added, and the government doesn’t value the natural resources found there. Since the nineties alone, nearly three hundred million acres of agricultural land across Europe have been abandoned. The trend is most pronounced in Mediterranean, Scandinavian, and Baltic countries, and it has several knock-on effects. Landscapes become more homogeneous, and vegetation gives way to shrubland. As traditional farming wanes, biodiversity tends to decrease—and wildfires tend to intensify. “The problem is that the fuel load has grown significantly over recent decades, mainly as a result of the exodus from rural areas,” Jesús Santiago Notario del Pino, a Spanish soil scientist and agricultural chemist, recently told the Spanish Science Media Center. “Something like this cannot be easily resolved in the short term.”

In the coming years, climate change and globalization are predicted to be the biggest drivers of continued land abandonment. Another risk factor, ironically, is rewilding—a conservation approach that aims to restore ecosystems to good health by reducing human interference. The long-term impacts of rewilding have not been well studied, and some scholars worry about it. A recent paper in the journal Ambio pointed out that, if a landscape has already been shaped by humans, an ideal of “wilderness” doesn’t necessarily make sense there. “Several ecosystems of high biodiversity value, often misclassified as ‘pristine,’ have been shaped over millennia of human use, a context rarely acknowledged by re-wilding approaches,” the paper argued. When it comes to fire management, the problem is that rewilding and land abandonment often resemble one another—shrubs encroach on open areas and forests grow denser. (In Ireland, more than half of land affected by wildfires over the past decade overlapped with Natura 2000 sites—protected nature areas created by the E.U.)

“Rewilding is seen by many people in a romantic way,” Alexander Held, a senior expert in fire management at the European Forest Institute, told me. Recent E.U. legislation mandates that twenty per cent of degraded land and sea areas be restored to a natural state by 2030, and that all ecosystems in need of repair be restored by 2050. Rewilding is a primary tool in this effort; some three hundred million acres in Europe have been identified as potential rewilding sites. But, if land is truly allowed to return to wilderness, a natural cycle of burning will also return—one that modern society may not be willing to tolerate.

Held favors an alternative model of forest conservation known as the close-to-nature movement, or “Pro Silva,” which advocates for human management of landscapes with natural processes in mind. Pro Silva practitioners view forests as holistic systems. Any activities in the forest—timber extraction, hunting—should be kept in balance for the sake of the over-all system. He argued that areas managed in this way are unusually resilient against the effects of climate change, including drought, storms, and fire. “This is a model where we can go into the future and have sustainable timber production, economic value, and nature conservation and biodiversity,” he said.

In Spain, there is a special term for land abandonment: la España vaciada. “It’s not only that they are empty but that they are being emptied,” Aragüés told me. Many of the places that have burned in the past two weeks fit this description. Orés, where about seventy people live, once had a population of many hundreds. The population of La Mierla has declined to just forty-four. Lands that are neither plantation nor agriculture, and that become overgrown through disuse, are known in Spain as monte. “Monte has more than doubled in the last fifty years,” Aragüés told me. “That is huge for a country like Spain. The abandonment is growing faster than we are able to manage the landscape.”

In most developed countries, policies tend to prioritize fire suppression over fire prevention. This has been true in Spain since at least the nineties. According to researchers at Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Spain spends an estimated 1.8 billion euros on fire management every year. Seventy-eight per cent goes to firefighting operations while twenty-two per cent goes to prevention. The emphasis on suppression, Aragüés said, may prevent residents of affected areas from feeling a sense of responsibility and ownership over fire prevention. “Now the local people, when they see a wildfire, they just expect helicopters and engines to solve that problem,” he said.

I was surprised that in my reporting, experts from different backgrounds agreed about several things. They warned that countries need to involve local people in their fire-management strategies, and to balance suppression with prevention. They argued that communities could reduce wildfire risks by managing lands and not letting them go wild. One way for European countries to prevent fires is by supporting rural livelihoods and traditional practices such as grazing, farming, forestry, and the intentional setting of controlled fires. If people want to keep conflagrations in check, nature needs people. “What people need to realize is that this is a structural issue in society,” a Spanish fire professional told me. “We’ve turned our backs on the mountains, on nature—and cities have never been so affected by it.”

In 2015, Aragüés left his job as a firefighter in Spain. Since then, he has worked in Indonesia, Ecuador, Chile, Portugal, and other countries with the aim of empowering local people to use fire as a land-management tool. Where controlled fires are set on purpose, uncontrolled fires are less likely to break out, and fire suppression can play a smaller role. “We cannot see another solution to this problem other than to develop local capacity in land and fire management,” he said. “We should learn from other places where we don’t have these strong suppression systems.”

Aragüés has been shocked by the fires across Europe. He has been thinking about a memorial in the forest that he and some crewmates built in 2005, after a fellow-firefighter died in the line of duty. Now the area was ablaze; Aragüés found out not long ago that, sadly, the memorial had burned. Even so, the mood of our conversation was not apocalyptic, and we tried to resist denial or despair. He told me about finding some measure of hope in a text message that his uncle, the retired firefighter, had sent him: “Mother Nature is more resilient. I think it’s going to teach us, like always, that there are other ways.” ♦

blocks.html_en: On July 22nd, sparks from a piece of heavy machinery ignited a fire near the town of Burgohondo, in Ávila province. blocks.html_en: In “Everything Must Go: The Stories We Tell About the End of the World,” the critic and journalist Dorian Lynskey points out that defeatism is unhelpful, and should not be mistaken for moral seriousness. “The evolutionary purpose of fear is to jolt one into an act of self-preservation,” Lynskey writes, “but one cannot live in a constant state of psychic emergency. The higher the stakes, the less tenable fear is, and the more likely it is to breed dissociation or hopelessness.” He instead calls on readers to resist—“to live in the space between ‘Everything will be OK’ and ‘Everything is fucked,’ between denial and despair.’ ” Lynskey suggests that there might be some way to grasp the significance of events like the unprecedented wildfires in Europe without giving in to dread. For me, the only way to do this is to get curious about why these things are happening. Why are flames erupting in this particular way, in this particular moment in time? Why is Europe burning?

blocks.html_en: In June, Stephen Pyne, a former wildland firefighter and an emeritus professor of history at Arizona State University, published his forty-sixth book, “Undying Fire: A Fire History of Europe.” When I called him, he posed me one of his central questions about megafires: “Why is it that countries that we think of as modernized—those that have money, science, technology—are the ones that are being clobbered?” Climate change is, of course, part of the story. “Fossil fuels give you power,” Pyne told me, but burning them “disrupts the climate in ways that make fires more powerful.” Extreme fire weather, exceptionally dry, windy, and often warm conditions, is on the rise globally. That said, climate change is happening everywhere—and, in Pyne’s account, only some areas are experiencing worsening fires. This is one of the mysteries he’s interested in.

blocks.html_en: Pyne argues that Mediterranean Europe, much like California, is naturally predisposed to burn because of an annual cycle of wetting and drying. He writes in “Undying Fire” that, for eons, Europeans used fire to cultivate pastures, farms, woodlands, gardens, and orchards; burning liberated nutrients, cleared space, and promoted desired plants. He calls this practice “pyric horticulture.” And many modern Europeans understand themselves as part of this history. A researcher examining attitudes about wildfire policy once interviewed a resident of the Occitanie region of southern France, which borders Spain. “We often forget that we are in a region, regardless of climate change, which experiences hot and dry summers, with fires which are very, very predominantly of anthropogenic origin,” the resident said. “And it doesn’t come from today, it comes from the time of the Romans and the Greeks.”

blocks.html_en: The most important way that European landscapes are changing is that unprecedented numbers of people are leaving rural areas, a phenomenon that has accelerated in the last fifty years. “Families leave the forests for the cities,” Mena, the firefighter in southern Spain, said. Jobs are scarce in rural areas, he added, and the government doesn’t value the natural resources found there. Since the nineties alone, nearly three hundred million acres of agricultural land across Europe have been abandoned. The trend is most pronounced in Mediterranean, Scandinavian, and Baltic countries, and it has several knock-on effects. Landscapes become more homogeneous, and vegetation gives way to shrubland. As traditional farming wanes, biodiversity tends to decrease—and wildfires tend to intensify. “The problem is that the fuel load has grown significantly over recent decades, mainly as a result of the exodus from rural areas,” Jesús Santiago Notario del Pino, a Spanish soil scientist and agricultural chemist, recently told the Spanish Science Media Center. “Something like this cannot be easily resolved in the short term.”

blocks.html_en: In the coming years, climate change and globalization are predicted to be the biggest drivers of continued land abandonment. Another risk factor, ironically, is rewilding—a conservation approach that aims to restore ecosystems to good health by reducing human interference. The long-term impacts of rewilding have not been well studied, and some scholars worry about it. A recent paper in the journal Ambio pointed out that, if a landscape has already been shaped by humans, an ideal of “wilderness” doesn’t necessarily make sense there. “Several ecosystems of high biodiversity value, often misclassified as ‘pristine,’ have been shaped over millennia of human use, a context rarely acknowledged by re-wilding approaches,” the paper argued. When it comes to fire management, the problem is that rewilding and land abandonment often resemble one another—shrubs encroach on open areas and forests grow denser. (In Ireland, more than half of land affected by wildfires over the past decade overlapped with Natura 2000 sites—protected nature areas created by the E.U.)

blocks.html_en: “Rewilding is seen by many people in a romantic way,” Alexander Held, a senior expert in fire management at the European Forest Institute, told me. Recent E.U. legislation mandates that twenty per cent of degraded land and sea areas be restored to a natural state by 2030, and that all ecosystems in need of repair be restored by 2050. Rewilding is a primary tool in this effort; some three hundred million acres in Europe have been identified as potential rewilding sites. But, if land is truly allowed to return to wilderness, a natural cycle of burning will also return—one that modern society may not be willing to tolerate.

He argued that areas managed in this way are unusually resilient against the effects of climate change, including drought, storms, and fire. “This is a model where we can go into the future and have sustainable timber production, economic value, and nature conservation and biodiversity,” he said.

blocks.html_en: In Spain, there is a special term for land abandonment: la España vaciada. “It’s not only that they are empty but that they are being emptied,” Aragüés told me. Lands that are neither plantation nor agriculture, and that become overgrown through disuse, are known in Spain as monte. “Monte has more than doubled in the last fifty years,” Aragüés told me. “That is huge for a country like Spain. blocks.html_en: In most developed countries, policies tend to prioritize fire suppression over fire prevention. This has been true in Spain since at least the nineties. According to researchers at Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Spain spends an estimated 1.8 billion euros on fire management every year. Seventy-eight per cent goes to firefighting operations while twenty-two per cent goes to prevention. blocks.html_en: I was surprised that in my reporting, experts from different backgrounds agreed about several things. blocks.html_en: Aragüés has been shocked by the fires across Europe. content_html_zh:
7月15日，西班牙北部萨拉戈萨省小镇奥雷斯附近爆发山火。 在强风和低湿度的推动下，火焰迅速蔓延到山麓和峡谷。 第二天，火势蔓延至一万一千多英亩，沿途五个城镇必须撤离。 何塞·路易斯·杜斯·阿拉圭斯 (José Luis Duce Aragüés) 是一位来自萨拉戈萨的荒野消防员，对于他来说，火灾的消息感觉很个人化。 十几岁的时候，他曾用夏天的时间探索那些现在正在燃烧的山脉。

仅仅两天后，阿拉圭斯（总部位于加利福尼亚州，但经常出差到世界各地帮助社区管理火灾风险）得知又发生了火灾。 这间位于附近的西班牙瓜达拉哈拉省，离他的家人今天居住的地方很近。 他在瓜达拉哈拉开始了他的消防生涯，夏天在科戈卢多小镇工作。 “我的一切都是从那里开始的，”阿拉圭斯告诉我。 “我在那里开始了我的镇压生涯——我的第一手机组人员、第一批发动机人员。 我熟悉那些山脉、那些森林、那些小径。” 拉米尔拉大火，后来被称为“拉米尔拉大火”，火势蔓延至八万多英亩。 他在该地区的许多朋友和家人要么撤离，要么努力扑灭大火。 他的叔叔是一名退休的荒地消防员，他用重型机械在他的农场周围修建了防火带，然后将其开到附近的村庄提供援助。 拉米尔拉大火的规模和猛烈程度让阿拉圭斯感到不安，但情况即将变得更糟。 “我不敢相信，当那场大火得到控制时，另一场火灾又发生了，”他说。

7月22日，一台重型机械产生的火花在阿维拉省布尔戈洪多镇附近引发火灾。 阿拉圭斯也曾在该领域为西班牙国家消防部队 Brigadas de Refuerzo en Incendios Forestales 以及该国环境部下属的防火小组工作过。 这一次，火焰蔓延并与马德里西南部山区附近已经燃烧的大火融合在一起。 大火最终蔓延到托莱多省，并发展成为布尔戈洪多火灾群——西班牙有记录以来最大的野火，覆盖面积超过十三万五千英亩。 一位科学家估计该建筑群释放的能量相当于二十三颗原子弹的能量。 阿拉圭斯了解到，他的一位前队友正在保卫朋友的房子，当大火沿着他旁边的斜坡蔓延时，他失去了自己的家。 另一位朋友，也是一名消防员，在火场附近给他发了一条短信：“何塞，我们所学到的一切，我们所知道的一切，我们 25 年来所学到的一切，都毫无意义。”

今年，西班牙已经有超过二十万公顷的土地被烧毁，这一数字是历史平均水平的两倍。 法国正在应对同样非同寻常的火灾季节。 波尔多以西的一场大火被描述为巴黎面积的四倍，引发了该国历史上和平时期最大规模的疏散：二十二万人。 与此同时，英国消防队员一直在努力控制廷特维斯尔沼泽火灾，这场火灾被认为是该国近代史上最大的火灾之一。 尽管气象学家警告说，一场“可怕的、持久的”热浪——欧洲今年的第四次热浪——即将到来，但北至瑞典、南至克里特岛的其他火灾仍在燃烧。

最近的一个晚上，可怕的新闻周期促使我打开 Instagram。 也许因为我自己就是一名合格的荒地消防员，所以我很快就被火灾的场景所震惊。 我看到马匹在幽灵般、烟雾缭绕的街道上逃命；无人机拍摄的烧焦的土地和房屋的外壳；火焰吞没了森林，警报声在远处响起。 许多蒙太奇都伴随着令人心碎的配乐。 经过一个小时的地狱般的主线图像之后，我感觉现实本身已经在火焰中燃烧了。 其中一个场景是橙色天空下燃烧的森林，上面覆盖着一个词：“启示录”。 当人类遭受灾难时，我感受到一种特殊的厄运感。

评论家兼记者多里安·林斯基（Dorian Lynskey）在《一切都必须过去：我们讲述的关于世界末日的故事》一书中指出，失败主义毫无帮助，不应被误认为是道德严肃性。 林斯基写道：“恐惧的进化目的是促使人采取自我保护的行为，但人不能生活在持续的精神紧急状态中。 风险越高，恐惧就越难以维持，就越有可能滋生分裂或绝望。” 相反，他呼吁读者抵制——“生活在‘一切都会好起来’和‘一切都完蛋’之间，否认和绝望之间。”林斯基建议，可能有某种方法可以抓住欧洲前所未有的野火等事件的重要性，而不屈服于恐惧。 对我来说，做到这一点的唯一方法就是好奇为什么会发生这些事情。 为什么火焰会在这个特定的时刻以这种特定的方式喷发？ 欧洲为何在燃烧？

当我向 Antonio J. 提出这个问题时 维拉·梅纳 (Vera Mena) 是一名西班牙荒地消防员，一直在安达卢西亚作为直升机旅的成员，他描述了一系列因素。 其中之一是极端炎热。 另一个矛盾之处是，最近一段时期异常潮湿，在已经杂草丛生的地区培育出茂密的草丛。 梅纳在一封电子邮件中说：“我们将所有这些成分放入鸡尾酒调酒器中，结果导致大火远远超出了消防队的灭火能力。”

六月，前荒地消防员、亚利桑那州立大学历史学名誉教授斯蒂芬·派恩出版了他的第四十六本书《不灭之火：欧洲火灾史》。 当我打电话给他时，他向我提出了关于特大火灾的核心问题之一：“为什么我们认为现代化的国家——那些拥有金钱、科学和技术的国家——却遭到了破坏？” 当然，气候变化是故事的一部分。 派恩告诉我：“化石燃料可以为你提供动力，但燃烧它们会破坏气候，从而使火势变得更猛烈。” 全球范围内极端干燥、多风且通常温暖的极端火灾天气正在增加。 也就是说，气候变化无处不在——而且，根据派恩的说法，只有某些地区的火灾正在恶化。 这是他感兴趣的谜团之一。

派恩认为，地中海欧洲就像加利福尼亚州一样，由于每年的干湿循环，自然容易发生火灾。 他在《不灭之火》中写道，千百年来，欧洲人用火来耕种牧场、农场、林地、花园和果园；燃烧释放的养分、清理空间并促进所需的植物生长。 他将这种做法称为“高温园艺”。 许多现代欧洲人将自己视为这段历史的一部分。 一位研究人们对野火政策态度的研究人员曾经采访过法国南部奥克西塔尼地区的一位居民，该地区与西班牙接壤。 这位居民说：“我们经常忘记，无论气候如何变化，我们所在的地区都会经历炎热干燥的夏季，火灾主要是人为原因造成的。” “它不是来自今天，而是来自罗马人和希腊人的时代。”

通过创造由连锁田地、牧场和果园组成的马赛克景观，欧洲人破坏并稀疏了树木和灌木丛，从而降低了发生毁灭性火灾的可能性。 但是，近几代以来，欧洲的乡村面貌发生了迅速变化。 农业产业化、规模化；快速生长的树木种植园已经蔓延。 社交媒体上一些最引人注目的镜头似乎显示了种植园森林的黑色残骸：一排又一排的树木，间隔均匀，就像爱荷华州的玉米一样，被火烧焦。

植树节常常受到庆祝，但细节很重要。 派恩认为，欧洲“破碎的生物群落”已经“转变为生物质燃料的单一种植”。 自 20 世纪 40 年代以来，仅西班牙就植树造林了约 400 万公顷——在历史上没有森林的地方建立了森林，其中大部分是松树和桉树等易燃树种。 1990 年至 2015 年间，欧洲森林面积增加了 9 万平方公里，相当于葡萄牙的国土面积。 欧盟承诺到 2030 年种植 30 亿棵树，以捕获和储存碳。 这一运动具有生态和社会后果，可燃性就是其中之一。

欧洲面貌发生变化的最重要方式是，空前数量的人口离开农村地区，这一现象在过去五十年中加速。 “很多家庭离开森林前往城市，”西班牙南部的消防员梅纳说。 他补充说，农村地区的就业机会稀缺，政府也不重视那里的自然资源。 仅自九十年代以来，欧洲就有近三亿英亩的农田被废弃。 这一趋势在地中海、斯堪的纳维亚和波罗的海国家最为明显，并产生了一些连锁反应。 景观变得更加均匀，植被被灌木丛所取代。 随着传统农业的衰落，生物多样性往往会减少，而野火往往会加剧。 西班牙土壤科学家和农业化学家赫苏斯·圣地亚哥·诺塔里奥·德尔·皮诺 (Jesús Santiago Notario del Pino) 最近告诉西班牙科学媒体中心：“问题在于，近几十年来，燃料负荷显着增加，这主要是由于农村地区的人口外流。” “这样的事情短期内不可能轻易解决。”

未来几年，气候变化和全球化预计将成为土地持续废弃的最大驱动因素。 具有讽刺意味的是，另一个风险因素是野化——一种旨在通过减少人类干扰来恢复生态系统健康的保护方法。 野化的长期影响尚未得到充分研究，一些学者对此表示担忧。 《Ambio》杂志最近发表的一篇论文指出，如果一片风景已经被人类塑造，那么“荒野”的理想在那里就不一定有意义了。 该论文指出，“几个具有高生物多样性价值的生态系统，经常被错误地归类为‘原始’，是在人类数千年的使用过程中形成的，而重新野化方法很少承认这一背景。” 在火灾管理方面，问题在于野化和土地废弃常常相似——灌木侵占空地，森林变得更加茂密。 （在爱尔兰，过去十年受野火影响的土地超过一半与 Natura 2000 地点（欧盟创建的自然保护区）重叠。）

“很多人都以一种浪漫的方式看待野化，”欧洲森林研究所火灾管理高级专家亚历山大·赫尔德告诉我。 最近的欧盟 立法规定到2030年将20%的退化土地和海域恢复到自然状态，到2050年恢复所有需要修复的生态系统。 野化是这项工作的主要工具；欧洲约三亿英亩土地已被确定为潜在的野化地点。 但是，如果真正允许土地回归荒野，燃烧的自然循环也会回归——这是现代社会可能不愿意容忍的。

霍尔德赞成另一种森林保护模式，称为“接近自然运动”或“Pro Silva”，该模式主张人类在管理景观时考虑到自然过程。 Pro Silva 的实践者将森林视为整体系统。 为了整个系统的利益，森林中的任何活动——木材采伐、狩猎——都应该保持平衡。 他认为，以这种方式管理的地区对气候变化的影响（包括干旱、风暴和火灾）具有异常的弹性。 “这是一个我们可以走向未来并拥有可持续木材生产、经济价值、自然保护和生物多样性的模式，”他说。

在西班牙，有一个专门的术语来形容土地废弃：la España vaciada。 “它们不仅是空的，而且正在被清空，”阿拉圭斯告诉我。 过去两周发生火灾的许多地方都符合这一描述。 奥雷斯居住着大约七十人，曾经有数百人。 拉米尔拉的人口已减少至仅四十四人。 既不是种植园也不是农业区且因闲置而变得杂草丛生的土地在西班牙被称为“monte”。 “过去五十年里，蒙特的股价增长了一倍多，”阿拉圭斯告诉我。 “这对于西班牙这样的国家来说意义重大。 废弃率的增长速度超过了我们管理景观的能力。”

在大多数发达国家，政策往往优先考虑灭火而不是预防。 至少从上世纪九十年代起，西班牙就是如此。 据圣地亚哥德孔波斯特拉大学的研究人员称，西班牙每年在火灾管理上的花费估计为 18 亿欧元。 78% 用于消防行动，22% 用于预防。 阿拉圭斯说，强调灭火可能会妨碍受影响地区的居民感受到防火的责任感和主人翁意识。 “现在当地人看到野火时，只希望直升机和发动机能够解决问题，”他说。

令我惊讶的是，在我的报告中，来自不同背景的专家在一些事情上达成了一致。 他们警告说，各国需要让当地人参与其火灾管理战略，并平衡抑制与预防。 他们认为，社区可以通过管理土地而不是让土地失控来减少野火风险。 欧洲国家预防火灾的方法之一是支持农村生计和传统做法，例如放牧、农业、林业和故意放火。 如果人们想要控制大火，大自然就需要人类。 “人们需要认识到，这是社会的结构性问题，”一位西班牙消防专业人士告诉我。 “我们已经背弃了山脉和自然，而城市从未受到如此大的影响。”

2015年，阿拉圭斯辞去了西班牙消防员的工作。 此后，他在印度尼西亚、厄瓜多尔、智利、葡萄牙和其他国家工作，旨在帮助当地人民使用火作为土地管理工具。 如果故意放火，那么失控的火灾就不太可能发生，灭火的作用也较小。 “除了发展当地土地和消防管理能力之外，我们看不到解决这个问题的其他方法，”他说。 “我们应该向其他没有这些强大压制系统的地方学习。”

阿拉圭斯对欧洲各地的大火感到震惊。 他一直在考虑在 2005 年一名消防员同事在执行任务时牺牲后，他和一些队友在森林里建造一座纪念碑。 现在这个地区已经着火了。阿拉圭斯不久前不幸地发现纪念碑已被烧毁。 即便如此，我们谈话的气氛并不是世界末日，我们试图抵制否认或绝望。 他告诉我，他在退休消防员叔叔发给他的短信中找到了一些希望：“大自然更具复原力。 我认为这将像往常一样告诉我们还有其他方法。” ❖
